title: The US-Canada Border Looks Drawn With a Ruler #shorts
summary: The 1818 Convention set the border on the 49th parallel from the Lake of the Woods to the Rockies; the 1846 Oregon Treaty extended it to the Pacific, leaving Vancouver Island British.
tags: why is the us canada border straight
sources: Treaty history: 1783 line from the northwesternmost point of Lake of the Woods due west to the Mississippi; 1818 Convention Article II, Lake of the Woods along the 49th parallel to the Stony Mountains (Rockies); 1846 Oregon Treaty westward along the 49th parallel to the Strait of Georgia, then through Juan de Fuca Strait to the Pacific; 1908 treaty for fuller demarcation; 1925 treaty changed the 49th parallel line from a slightly curved line between monuments to a series of straight lines (International Boundary Commission, History): https://internationalboundarycommission.org/en/about/history.php

Convention of 1818, Article II: a line drawn from the most North Western Point of the Lake of the Woods along the forty Ninth Parallel of North Latitude ... from the Lake of the Woods to the Stony Mountains; signed London, 20 October 1818 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School): https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/conv1818.asp

Oregon Treaty, Article I: the line of boundary shall be continued westward along the said forty-ninth parallel of north latitude to the middle of the channel which separates the continent from Vancouver's Island, and thence southerly ... through Fuca's Straits to the Pacific Ocean; signed Washington, 15 June 1846 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School): https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/br-1846.asp

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html

scenes.narration: This border looks like someone drew it with a ruler.
Across the West, it follows one line of latitude: the {49th|forty-ninth} parallel.
In {1818|eighteen eighteen}, Britain and the US picked it, from the Lake of the Woods to the Rockies.
In {1846|eighteen forty-six}, they ran it to the Pacific. And Britain kept all of Vancouver Island.
